lessons.intro: You will learn what a magnet attracts and how two magnets behave together.

paragraphs: A [magnet] is a special object. It can [attract] some things. A nail or a [paper clip] flies to the [magnet] and can [stick] to it.
A [magnet] attracts only some [metal] things. It likes [iron] and steel. It does not attract [plastic], [wood], glass or paper. Try it at home!
Not every [metal] is magnetic. Aluminium foil and copper coins do not [stick] to a [magnet]. Only some metals feel the magnet's power.
Every [magnet] has two ends. We call them the [north pole] and the [south pole]. Each [pole] is usually a different colour.
Now take two magnets. A [north pole] and a [south pole] [attract] each other. Two same poles [push away] each other. Try it!

lessons.intro: You will learn that a magnet pulls things from a distance and how to compare two magnets.

paragraphs: A [magnet] does not need to touch things. It can [attract] a [paper clip] from a small [distance]. The invisible space around a magnet is called the [magnetic field].
You cannot see the [magnetic field]. But you can see what it does. The clip moves and jumps. The field is strongest close to the [magnet] and weaker far away.
A magnet pulls [iron] and steel. It does not pull [plastic], [wood], paper or glass. Try it at home with safe objects.
Here is an [experiment]. Put a [paper clip] on the table. Move the magnet slowly closer. Stop when the clip jumps. Measure the [distance] with a [ruler].
Now test a second magnet the same way. A [strong] magnet pulls the clip from farther away. A [weak] magnet must be very close.

lessons.intro: You will learn what a compass is and how it shows direction.

paragraphs: A [compass] is a small tool. Inside it there is a thin [needle]. The [needle] is a small [magnet]. It can turn freely and it always stops in the same [direction].
The [Earth] works like a big [magnet]. That is why the coloured end of the [needle] points to the [north]. Opposite to [north] is [south]. On the left is [west] and on the right is [east].
A [hiker] puts the [compass] flat on the hand. He waits until the [needle] stops. Then he knows the [direction] and he can read his [map].
People use a [compass] in a big [forest], in the mountains or on a boat. A [compass] needs no batteries. But keep it away from a strong [magnet] or iron, because they move the [needle].

lessons.intro: Learn how machines help us lift and move heavy things.

paragraphs: Simple machines help us do work with less [force]. We use them every day!
A [lever] is a long bar. It turns on a [fulcrum]. A longer lever needs less force to lift a heavy [load]. A seesaw and [scissors] are levers.
An [inclined plane] is a slope. It is easier to push a box up a slope than to lift it. A [screw] and an [axe] are inclined planes too.
A [pulley] is a wheel with a rope. We pull the rope down and the load goes up. A [crane] uses pulleys.
A [gear] is a wheel with teeth. Gears turn other gears. You can find gears in a [bicycle] and in a clock.

lessons.intro: You learn how to make dots with many tools and how to build pictures and stories from dots.

paragraphs: A [dot] is the smallest mark in art. You make a [dot] when you [press] a [pencil], a [brush] or your [finger] on paper. Dots are easy and fun.
Dots are not all the same. They have a different [size] and colour. A [sponge] makes a big soft dot. A sharp [pencil] makes a tiny dot.
Many dots close together look dark. Far away dots look light. This is called [texture]. A [row of dots] looks like a line, so you can draw with dots only.
Some painters paint whole pictures with small colour dots. This is [pointillism]. Printers also use a [grid] of tiny dots. Look at a comic picture with a magnifier.
Dots can tell a story. A white dot can be a [star] in space. Small dark dots can be a meadow grasshopper jumping in the grass.
reading.title: The Magic of Dots

lessons.intro: You will learn how to draw shadows with lines using hatching and shading.

paragraphs: First you draw a [still life] or a [landscape] with a simple [line]. The line shows the shape. Then you make some parts dark and some parts bright.
[hatching] means many short lines next to each other. Close lines look dark. Lines far apart look bright. This is how you show a [shadow].
[cross-hatching] means lines in two directions. They cross like a net. It looks darker than simple hatching.
[shading] is different. You use a soft [pencil] and rub it. It is smooth, with no lines. With [ink] you can only use lines, not smooth shading.
Change your [pressure]. Strong pressure is dark, soft pressure is bright. The [light] side stays white. Lines can also show [texture], like fur or wood.

lessons.intro: You will learn party and drama words and act out a birthday guest.

paragraphs: It is my [birthday]. I have a [party] at school. Every [guest] comes to the door. But nobody says a name. It is a fun [role play] game.

lessons.intro: You will learn colour words and say how colours make people feel.

paragraphs: An [artist] uses [colour] like words. Red, orange and yellow are [warm colours]. They look like fire and sun. Blue, green and purple are [cool colours]. They look like water and ice.
A [bright] [colour] often shows a happy [feeling]. A [dark] [colour] can show a quiet or sad [feeling]. The [background] is important too. A grey sky makes a [painting] look cold.
You can [mix] colours. Blue and yellow make green. Red and yellow make orange. Take a clean [brush] and try it. Wash the [brush] between colours.
Now [paint] your own picture. Choose colours for your [feeling] today. Two people can [paint] the same tree in different colours. Both pictures are good. There is no wrong [colour].
reading.title: How Do Colours Speak?

lessons.intro: You will revise school words, frequency adverbs, the word who, and colours.

paragraphs: My name is Ema. Every Monday I look at my [timetable]. I [always] have [maths] first. Numbers are fun, but big sums are [difficult] for me.
On Tuesday we have [science]. We look at leaves and water. Science is [exciting] because we do experiments. I [sometimes] write my notes in green pen.
My favourite lesson is [art]. My teacher is a man [who] paints big pictures. Our classroom is bright and [colourful]. I [never] feel bored there.
In [art] we learn about the three [primary colours]: red, blue and yellow. We mix them. Blue and yellow make green. Red and yellow make orange.
Colours help us. Red can say 'Stop!' Blue can feel calm and cool. Artists use colours to show feelings in their pictures.

prompts.answer: We use 'who' to say more about a person. Example: This is my friend who plays the guitar. Example: I know a girl who always helps me.

prompts.answer: One: warm colours like red and orange show energy. Two: cool colours like blue show calm. Three: mix colours to make new ones for your feeling.
